summary: Defines the View-based Access Control Model for SNMP, which controls who may read or change which pieces of management information. It specifies the elements of procedure and includes a MIB to configure the model remotely. It replaces RFC 2575.

plainLanguage.summary: VACM is an access-control model for SNMP management data. It checks the user's security identity, the context and security level, and the requested operation before allowing access to an object.

questions: what is a mib view in snmp
how does snmp access control work
subtitle: How SNMP maps a security identity and operation to permitted management data.

tldr.problem: An SNMP engine needs a consistent way to decide whether a principal may read, change, or send a notification about a particular management object.
tldr.mechanism: VACM maps a security model and name to a group, selects an access entry using context and security level, then checks the object against the read, write, or notify view.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3415 is Internet Standard STD 62 and obsoletes RFC 2575. It includes a MIB for remotely managing VACM configuration.

today: RFC 3415 is Internet Standard STD 62, published in December 2002, and obsoletes RFC 2575. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: VACM in the SNMP Architecture
sections.content:
The SNMP Access Control Subsystem decides whether a request may read or write an object, or include it in a notification. RFC 3415 defines the View-based Access Control Model (VACM), one model that applications can call when making those decisions.

The calling application is responsible for requesting an access check. VACM keeps its policy in the engine's Local Configuration Datastore. The RFC includes a Management Information Base (MIB) module so portions of that configuration can be managed remotely.
sections.plainLanguage: VACM checks whether an SNMP operation may access a particular management object. SNMP applications call it, and its rules are stored in the engine's configuration.

sections.title: Groups, Security Levels, and Contexts
sections.content:
A group collects zero or more pairs of security model and security name. Each pair maps to at most one group. VACM assumes that another part of SNMP has already authenticated the security name; VACM does not authenticate it itself.

Rules may vary by security level: noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv, or authPriv. A context is a collection of management information available through an SNMP entity. The same information may appear in more than one context.
sections.plainLanguage: VACM puts security identities into groups and can give each group different rights at different security levels. A context identifies the set of management information being checked.

sections.title: Views of Management Information
sections.content:
A MIB view defines which managed object instances a group may access in a context. A view can include or exclude subtrees in the object identifier tree. A subtree represents objects whose identifiers share a prefix.

A view-tree family combines a subtree with a bit mask. A mask bit of one requires the corresponding identifier component to match; a zero acts as a wildcard. The access policy selects separate views for reading, writing, and sending notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A view is a defined set of management objects that a group may access. A mask can describe a family of related object identifiers without listing each one separately.

sections.title: How VACM Makes an Access Decision
sections.content:
The isAccessAllowed service receives the security model, security name, security level, requested view type, context name, and object identifier. VACM first checks that the context exists. It then maps the security identity to a group and finds an access entry for that group, context, security model, and security level.

The requested operation selects the read, write, or notify view. VACM checks whether the object identifier belongs to that view. It returns accessAllowed if it does; missing contexts, groups, entries, or views produce distinct errors, and an object outside the view produces notInView.
sections.plainLanguage: VACM checks the context, group, access rule, and requested view in sequence. It allows the operation only if the target object is included in that view.

sections.title: The Configuration MIB
sections.content:
The SNMP-VIEW-BASED-ACM-MIB stores the information VACM uses. Its tables list local contexts, map security identities to groups, assign access entries, and define included or excluded view subtrees. An access entry contains the read, write, and notify view names.

An access entry can match a context exactly or by prefix. When several entries match, VACM prefers a specific security model over any, a matching context, the longest context prefix, and then the highest applicable security level. The MIB also defines an advisory lock to help management applications coordinate view changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB stores contexts, group membership, access rules, and view definitions in separate tables. When multiple rules could apply, VACM chooses the most specific matching rule.

sections.title: Protecting VACM Policy
sections.content:
VACM trusts the calling module to provide the authentication and privacy level it reports. Administrators must use access-table security levels to distinguish unauthenticated access from authenticated access, because group membership itself does not include a security level.

Changing included and excluded view entries in the wrong order can temporarily grant unwanted access. The configuration MIB controls access to all SNMP management data and may be sensitive, so both reading and writing it should be closely controlled. A conforming implementation must implement the MIB according to its compliance statement.
sections.plainLanguage: VACM does not verify identity itself, so it relies on the security information supplied by SNMP. Administrators should protect the policy tables because changing them can change access to managed data.
